question.problem:
Consider the orthogonal set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3},\,{x}_{4}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}.$ What is the value of $\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{3}}?$

$$
U=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}
$$
question.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2},\,{u}_{3}.$ To extend the given set to an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}$, we need to find a fourth vector $x$ such that

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{3}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{4}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{4}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}+{x}_{4}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{21}{5} & \frac{6}{5} & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:=-\frac{5}{21}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{2}{7} & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are three pivot columns ($1$st, $2$nd and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{4}$ is a free variable. From the second and third equations, we get ${x}_{2}=\frac{1}{7}{x}_{4}$ and ${x}_{3}=\frac{2}{7}{x}_{4}$, respectively. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{7}{x}_{4}+{x}_{4}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-\frac{6}{7}{x}_{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{6}{7}{x}_{4} \\ \frac{1}{7}{x}_{4} \\ \frac{2}{7}{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{4}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{4}=7,$ we obtain the vector 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ 7\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}$ is

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -4 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{3}}=\frac{1}{2}.$
